subject: Accounting
title: Cost of Goods Sold
description: A 60-second lesson on Cost of Goods Sold.

hook.text: Revenue looks great until you subtract what it cost to deliver. That's cost of goods sold.

buildup.text: COGS includes raw materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead tied to products sold.

discovery.text: Gross profit = Revenue minus COGS. It shows how much money production itself generates.

twist.text: A company with $10 million in revenue but $9.5 million in COGS barely has room to breathe.

climax.text: Managing COGS is where operational efficiency meets financial performance.

punchline.text: Revenue is vanity. COGS reveals the real margin.

quiz.question: What does COGS measure?
options: The direct cost of producing goods that were sold

details.summary: Cost of goods sold represents the direct costs of producing the goods a company sells—materials, labor, and manufacturing overhead. This topic explains how COGS is calculated, how it differs by costing method, and its impact on gross profit.
details.whyItMatters: COGS is the largest expense for most product-based businesses and directly determines gross profit. Getting it wrong means every profitability analysis built on it is unreliable.
takeaways: COGS includes direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead for units sold
Different inventory methods—FIFO, LIFO, weighted average—produce different COGS figures
COGS appears on the income statement and is subtracted from revenue to calculate gross profit

faq.question: What is cost of goods sold?
faq.answer: Cost of goods sold is the total cost of producing the products a company sold during a period. It includes direct materials, direct labor, and allocated manufacturing overhead. COGS is subtracted from revenue on the income statement to determine gross profit.

faq.question: How does inventory method affect cost of goods sold?
faq.answer: FIFO assigns the oldest inventory costs to COGS (lower COGS when prices rise), LIFO assigns the newest costs (higher COGS when prices rise), and weighted average blends all costs. The choice directly affects reported profit and tax liability.
